text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG

- NATO and Russia launch the start of their new partnership with the signing of the Foundation Act in Paris and an unscheduled pledge by Russian President Boris Yeltsin to dismantle all warheads directed at western targets.

- The business of spying featured little in the trial of legendary East German spymaster Markus Wolf, sentenced to a two-year suspended sentence on charges of kidnapping, coercion and bodily harm, crimes the result of Cold War intrigues between the east and west of the country.

- French President Chirac, reeling from the weak showing of his government in the first round of French elections, steps in to pledge tax cuts and asks the French in return to give him a workable majority for the next five years.
BUSINESS STORIES

- German post office says its plans to be privatised and seek a listing on the bourse could be endangered by a new post bill going much further in opening the German market up to competition than European Union rules envisage.
HANDELSBLATT
- Yeltsin promises that Russian nuclear weapons will never again pose a threat to NATO, but the planned eastwards expansion of the NATO block remains a bone of contention.
- France's Chirac warns against a return to socialism in France, arguing that a defeat for his current government in election rounds to come could damage France's place in Europe.
- The BDI German employers federation urges government and opposition SPD politicians to agree on the major tax reform plan as soon as possible.
BUSINESS
- With yawning holes in its federal budget, Bonn must move to accelerate the privatisation of state-owned motorway service activities
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Yeltsin promise: nuclear weapons no longer to be targeted at NATO countries

- International sponsors for the reconstruction of Bosnia are losing patience with the failure of Serbs, Muslims and Croats to cooperate and will urge a greater push to implement the Dayton agreement later this week at the NATO spring conference.
BUSINESS
- German post office chief Klaus Zumwinkel warns that plans by Bonn to restrict its monopoly more tightly than that of post services elsewhere in Europe threatened its planned bourse listing.
DIE WELT
- Yeltsin signs deal with NATO, leaving way for eastward expansion of treaty organisation free.
- U.S. court allows sexual harassment lawsuit to go ahead
BUSINESS
- In an "act of will without parallel", Germans have paid a trillion marks in the last seven years to rebuild East Germany following unification, a government politician said.
